question.text: Mr. Ramesh Iyer is explaining to a first-time LP why 'Lotus India Growth AIF' (Cat II) uses a pooled vehicle instead of managing each investor's money in a separate portfolio. Which of the following is the MOST accurate rationale for pooling in an AIF context?

answer.text: Pooling guarantees each investor a separately managed, customised mandate (like PMS) with individual portfolio statements.
Pooling is a SEBI-mandated requirement only for Category III AIFs and is optional for Category I and II.
Pooling eliminates the need for the manager to draft a Private Placement Memorandum (PPM) because all investors share a single mandate.
Pooling combines investor contributions into a common corpus to achieve economies of scale, risk diversification and collective investment management ('blind-pool investing').

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the workbook (pages 96-97), pooling is central to AIF structuring: investor contributions are combined into a common corpus or blind pool managed under a single mandate, enabling economies of scale, risk diversification and collective investment management. Individual customisation is the hallmark of portfolio management services, not pooled AIFs. The PPM (page 94) remains the offer document regardless of pooling. The Trap: The PMS-like option confuses pooling with portfolio management. The Cat III-only option wrongly carves out Cat I/II. The PPM-waiver option is false because the PPM is the AIF's offer document and is not displaced by pooling. Note: The pooling rationale (economies of scale, diversification, blind-pool investing) is from pages 96-97; the PPM-as-offer-document reference is on page 94.
